original_value: AbstractClassification of electrocardiogram (ECG) signals is obligatory for the automatic diagnosis of cardiovascular disease. With the recent advancement of low‐cost wearable ECG device, it becomes more feasible to utilize ECG for cardiac arrhythmia classification in daily life. In this paper, we propose a lightweight approach to classify five types of cardiac arrhythmia, namely, normal beat (N), atrial premature contraction (A), premature ventricular contraction (V), left bundle branch block beat (L), and right bundle branch block beat (R). The combined method of frequency analysis and Shannon entropy is applied to extract appropriate statistical features. Information gain criterion is employed to select features that the results show that 10 highly effective features can obtain performance measures comparable to those obtained by using the complete features. The selected features are then fed to the input of Random Forest, K‐Nearest Neighbour, and J48 for classification. To evaluate classification performance, tenfold cross validation is used to verify the effectiveness of our method. Experimental results show that Random Forest classifier demonstrates significant performance with the highest sensitivity of 98.1%, the specificity of 99.5%, the precision of 98.1%, and the accuracy of 98.08%, outperforming other representative approaches for automated cardiac arrhythmia classification.

result.paraphrase: ECG signal classification is essential for automated cardiovascular disease diagnosis. With the latest low-cost wearable ECG devices, using ECG for everyday cardiac arrhythmia classification has become more practical. In this paper, we present a lightweight method for identifying five arrhythmia classes: normal beat (N), atrial premature contraction (A), premature ventricular contraction (V), left bundle branch block beat (L), and right bundle branch block beat (R). Appropriate statistical features are extracted using a combination of frequency analysis and Shannon entropy. Feature selection is performed with the information gain criterion, and the results indicate that 10 highly effective features can achieve performance comparable to using the full feature set. These selected features are then supplied to Random Forest, K-Nearest Neighbour, and J48 classifiers. Tenfold cross validation is used to assess performance and confirm the method’s effectiveness. Experimental results show that Random Forest achieves the best results, with sensitivity of 98.1%, specificity of 99.5%, precision of 98.1%, and accuracy of 98.08%, outperforming other representative approaches for automated cardiac arrhythmia classification.
